- So again, we're not raising these to make you go back to your organizations and be suspicious of everybody, but it is your responsibility to make sure that there are strategies and understandings in place throughout the organization for the protection of the organization, but also individuals.
    
- So, keeping an eye out for, you know, individuals that, you know, maybe have
    
- significant changes, unexpectedly, or, you know, like to keep their role very, isolated, and especially if they're having something to do with the money. But there's a lot of really
    
- Simple strategies that you can build into your operations and your processes to make sure that, any kind of fraud is, activity is limited and hopefully avoided completely.
    
- So what we recommend should be in front of the board at every meeting.
    
- Is a statement of financial position, so your balance sheet, so people understand what the organization owns and owes.
    
- A statement of financial performance, the profit loss compared to the budget, so you can monitor, the performance of the organization and ask some key questions.
    
- A forecast through to the end of the year, and this might look like, kind of, cash flows forecast to have a good understanding of, the ups and downs and how, you know, how solvent the organization is and any risks.
    
- Commentary on variances and the assumptions behind them, so not leaving the board to guess, but providing context and understanding, and your expertise understanding on the financial performance and position.
    
- And an up-to-date download of current bank account statements. It's very simple, just so that you can, everyone can validate that what is on the reports is actually reflected in the bank.
    
- And it's important to present this in a way that works for the least financially literate person on the board.
    
- I'm not suggesting you ask people to rate their financial literacy, you know, but important to think, okay, well, we need to make sure everyone understands this, so even asking, would you like graphs? Would you like me to provide a summary? What would you need to make sure that you have a really informed financial position at every board meeting?
    
- So, most of the budget process is guessing, and sometimes you guess wrongly. So, in procedural terms, your chance to probe these issues in detail comes when you're putting together, say, a finance or business plan.
    
- And this plan puts meat on the skeleton of your strategic plan, spelling out how you'll get from where you are at the moment to where you want to be in your glorious organisational's future. And like a long-term strategy, this looks ahead, sort of 3 to 5 years, and you would refresh it when you do your, strategic plan.
    
- You don't have to do this, but it is a good idea of just having that long-term, sustainability.
    
- So, it's important to think about, these sorts of questions.
    
- Are we generating enough income to cover the work that we need to do?
    
- And if we're losing money, do we have enough reserves to cover it, or do we have enough savings to invest in the organization?
    
- How much does it actually cost to progress our mission, or progress our purpose?
    
- Is our budget sustainable? Are we including enough costs for administration, evaluation, and planning? Often, not-for-profits are scraping, you know, the barrel, but it's important that we are
    
- Covering the actual cost of the work that needs to be done, and we're not, at risk of burning out all our staff either.
    
- Can we pay our debts now and in the future? How sustainable is our income?
    
- And how quickly could we access our reserves if we suddenly needed to? So again, that understanding of current and non-current assets, if we suddenly had a major cash flow problem, how quickly could we,
    
- Liquify? I don't think that's the right word. Make liquid our, our non-current assets. If we had to sell things, what would that look like? And putting those plans in place before you hit the kind of tough periods.
    
- So, really important that, and again, this is not just the work of the Treasurer. This should be a partnership with the rest of the board, as well as the, executive leadership of the operational team.
    
- In small, not-for-profits, that might look like, you know, a couple of key volunteers, but to really be able to answer those questions and get a good understanding of where your organization is at now, but also in the future.
    
- So…
    
- When you're thinking about how sustainable your income is, often not-for-profits are reliant on one or two major income sources, be it grants or donations or membership. So, it's important to have an understanding of what proportion of your income comes from your largest funder or income stream.
    
- Have the conversation and thinking around if that source disappeared, could you survive and how long?
    
- And what do we need to do about actively diversifying, reliance on funding from one source into different, sources? Especially because that can take a bit of time to do.
    
- And then finally, does our reserve policy account for this risk? So, if we've got a reserves policy, are we thinking about, you know, investment in our own organization? Do we have a plan for what it's there for?
    
- A few other things, to make sure that you're looking at and asking about. Aged creditors. So, how long do we take to pay debts? Are we a bit slow in our bill paying?
    
- This can be obviously not great in terms of our reputation, but also might point to some, procedure or process or policy that's not working effectively.
    
- Also, how long do we take to get paid the money that we are, owed? If that's a bit of a struggle, and that's going higher and higher each time you get your balance sheet, again, something to look at in terms of process or, you know, perhaps even the debtors or the organizations you're working with.
    
- Are they reliable?
    
- do we have to think about different contractors? So, all those sorts of questions. Again, we're not asking these to put blame on anybody, we're asking these to develop a better understanding.
    
- And cash flow projection. Again, depending on your organization, but if you've got some sort of, you know, kind of, shop or, not commercial side, but some sort of, more active cash flow side that's not just relying on regular payments.
    
- then it's very important to have an understanding of the cash flow projections over the next few months, so that you're not just kind of scrambling. You do have a good idea of when money's coming in, when it needs to go out, and how that's being managed.
    
- Are we compliant with regulatory requirements? So first of all, knowing what they are. We have a compliance calendar, that you can download on, Community Directors' website as well, that will give you a very comprehensive understanding of lots of different compliance obligations.
    
- But you can edit it to pick the ones that are most, relevant and useful to your particular situation.
    
- And are we discharging our duties for superannuation and portable long service leave, if appropriate?
    
- The, superannuation payments changed relatively recently as well, so again, if you're overseeing finances, important to just check that that has been updated, and if you're the one doing the financial management, doing the books.
    
- Then important that you're on top of any changes that happen.
    
- So good to just be connected with, kind of, you know, maybe CPA Australia, or, you know, key banks, newsletters, and the ATO to keep on top of any, regulatory obligations that change.
    
- And finally, every Treasurer's term ends eventually. You will not be Treasurer forever, some of you might be disappointed, and some of you might be slightly relieved by that.
    
- But it will happen. So, it's important to think about how you leave the organization, and particularly your role, in good shape.
    
- And the key is to start with a plan early.
    
- even as soon as you become the Treasurer, start planning what you will hand over when you leave. We're all human, we never know when that time may be, so it's good to have things in place as quick as possible.
    
- So part of this is around succession planning. As Treasurer, keep an eye on who's in your organization's volunteer pool, and start thinking about a pathway that might work for them. So they might be not ready to join the board at the next AGM,
    
- But they might be willing to join a subcommittee, or, you know, come and see some board meetings as an observer, or just be involved a little bit more in the organization.
    
- again, a finance subcommittee, if you've got one that has, people… well, even people on the board that are definitely, you know, showing an interest in the finance side of things, usually the first place to look. But don't assume that someone on the finance committee is going to step up for the job.
    
- And if someone is interested, then if you can, take the time to mentor them and really, you know, show them the ropes of the role.
    
- Bringing someone in cold with no governance or finance, grounding, while that happens, let's be honest, the not-for-profit sector often it is about bums on seats sometimes.
    
- But people need training, so even if they don't have a lot of experience, there is training out there, so make sure that there's, time, and they have the opportunities to access that. Again, it's important for the board as individuals, because you have that legal responsibility.
    
- But, most importantly, you want to leave your organization in a better position than you found it.
    
- And don't leave them alone. Even the most experienced treasurer, you know, you can get a…
    
- highly experienced, certified accountant, but your organization will be new to them. Processes will be new, culture will be new, so it's important that there's a really good, thorough, induction process, onboarding, and that people feel part of the organization, part of the board.
    
- And not just there for their financial skills.
    
- So, in summary, as Treasurer, you are the first among equals in financial governance.
    
- You probably have more expertise, though, but it's important that you share that, and you don't hoard it. Again, you're thinking about how you want to hand over your role.
    
- Your role is to guide and support decision making, not lead it. So you shouldn't be coming to board meetings and saying, right, I'm the Treasurer, this is what we need to do. It's very much in that guiding role.
    
- As I mentioned earlier, make sure financial information is suitable for the least confident member, and encourage silly questions.
    
- If you set up effective systems, structures, and processes early on, then it will make not just your life, but everyone that comes after you in the Treasurer's role much easier.
    
- So, thank you all so much. I know that was a lot of information.
